newSounds: Five pure vowels a/e/i/o/u = ah/eh/ee/oh/oo (like Telugu అ ఎ ఈ ఒ ఊ), no diphthongs and every vowel is spoken. ng as in sing (no hard g), ny as in onion, ch as in church, sh as in ship, th as in think (dh as in the), gh a throaty g, r rolled like Telugu ర.
rhythm: Syllable-timed and regular: mostly consonant+vowel beats with stress on the second-last syllable of each word -- very close to Telugu, so the rhythm is easy for you.
registerFirst: Polite plural first: m-/mu- verb prefixes and nyinyi (with -lenu/-yenu) for strangers, elders and officials; u-/wewe is for friends and family. Add respect words baba, mama, bwana, bibi, daktari, mwalimu; Shikamoo greets an elder.
trap: No tones and no gendered verbs, but noun classes drive agreement (ki-/vi- chumba -> kiko/kina, li- duka -> liko, m- daktari -> yuko). 'za/ya' mean 'of', and 'saa mbili' is 8 a.m., not 2.
